title: The Seat You Can't Fill by March: Canadian Driver Licensing Decisions for 2027
summary: Ontario's Jan. 1 Class A wait, Quebec's retest, Alberta's Bill 43 and new LMIA rules reshape Canadian driver hiring for 2027. What fleets should decide now.
body_markdown:
It's Monday morning, and the whiteboard in your office says "2027 seats: 9."


You run safety and driver recruiting for a mid-size Ontario fleet. About 110 tractors, a terminal in the GTA, a smaller one outside Montreal, a handful of drivers based in Calgary for western cross-border work.


Sales just signed Ontario-Quebec dedicated freight starting in March. Two senior drivers retire in February. You need nine qualified drivers in seats by spring.


You have 14 candidates. You check each against the rules landing in the next 100 days.


By lunch, the 14 are down to five you can count on for March.


(The fleet is illustrative. The rules are not.)


## The wall that lands on Jan. 1


Start with your strongest group: four candidates finishing Class A training in January. Three got their full Class G this past summer.


Ontario's Ministry of Transportation is adding a mandatory six-month waiting period, effective Jan. 1, 2027, before Class G or higher licence holders can attempt a Class A road test, per the province's Sept. 21, 2026 release.


What it means: a candidate who finishes training in January but got a full G in August can't take a road test until about February. For you, that's a March seat at best, with no room for a failed attempt.


Here's the catch. Per the ministry's rule as reported in trade coverage, the wait applies to road tests taken on or after Jan. 1. A test passed in December runs under today's rules.


So, December road tests or wait? Push only the candidates who are genuinely ready. Fail in January and it's not a quick retake. You're locked out until the six months are done.


The same Sept. 21 release says every training provider will have to teach a new standardized entry-level curriculum of "more than 103 hours," with implementation expected to begin early in 2027.


What it means: the hours floor isn't really rising. Ontario's minimum entry-level training is already 103.5 hours. What's changing is that every school must teach the same thing, which makes shortcuts easier to spot.


## Why the province stopped trusting the paperwork


You've seen it. A new hire with a fresh licence who can't back a 53-footer into a door.


Ontario's Auditor General explained why in a May 12, 2026 report on commercial truck driver licensing. Undercover students at six training providers found two private career colleges delivering just 59.5 and 81 hours of instruction, against the 103.5-hour minimum. As of March 2025, 54 of 216 registered private career colleges offering entry-level truck training had never been inspected.


What it means: a licence alone doesn't tell you what a driver was taught. Your road test and yard evaluation are doing work the system was supposed to do.


Two of your 14 trained at a school you've never heard of, with thin hours paperwork. You don't reject them. You move them into a longer in-house finishing program. They become summer seats, not March seats.


## The Quebec lane that changed the math


Next problem. The new freight runs out of your Montreal-area terminal, and three candidates plan to move there. All three got their Ontario Class A less than two years ago.


Since July 2026, Quebec's licensing authority, the SAAQ, requires Ontario Class 1 holders with under 24 months of Class 1 experience to pass Quebec's practical exams before exchanging their licence for a Quebec one, per the Quebec government's July 2026 announcement. Fail twice and the driver has to complete Quebec's mandatory Class 1 training, which has been in place since Dec. 15, 2025.


Quebec calls the measure temporary.


What it means: a driver who moves to Quebec for your terminal may face a road test there before they're licensed as a resident. Book that test into your onboarding plan, and have a backup driver for the first weeks of the lane.


One plans to keep living in Ontario. Two are moving. They go on the board with a question mark.


## The restricted licence nobody flagged


Your western team sends two Calgary candidates, both newly licensed in Alberta. Both look great on paper.


Alberta replaced its old entry-level program with a Class 1 Learning Pathway on April 1, 2025. A new driver who completes the Entry and Core Learning programs and passes the road test gets a Class 1 licence restricted to driving in Alberta, per the province's program page. The restriction comes off only after a Competence Building Program of 10 to 18 hours of one-on-one instruction, based on an on-road assessment.


What it means: a fresh Alberta Class 1 can't run your Calgary to B.C. or Saskatchewan freight yet. If dispatch doesn't know that, you'll find out from an inspector.


So those two seats exist, but only for Alberta-only work. You don't have much of that.


## Alberta wants your name on a list


On Nov. 19, 2026, Alberta introduced Bill 43, the Safe and Sensible Roads Act. It would raise maximum fines for major commercial vehicle incidents, including bridge strikes and repeated safety violations, from $10,000 to $50,000, per trade reporting on the bill. It would also allow commercial licence downgrades, with conditions such as retraining.


The bill's text goes further. It would let the province publicly release information on carriers, commercial drivers, schools and inspection facilities. For a carrier, that could mean its name, safety fitness certificate number, region and type of contravention.


Bill 43 isn't law yet, and the province hasn't announced when the trucking measures would take effect.


What it means: a driver downgrade becomes an instant empty seat. Public naming means shippers, brokers and insurers will see your record without asking you for it.


Alberta said in an August 2026 update that since October 2025 it had removed 20 trucking companies from its roads, 13 of them chameleon carriers, issued 443 administrative penalties and shut down five fraudulent Class 1 driver training schools, per trade reporting of that update.


What it means: your Alberta drivers' training history now matters as much as their abstract. And if you run a brokerage desk, a public list is one more record shippers will expect you checked.


## The immigration math changes in March


You still need nine seats, so you look at the Temporary Foreign Worker Program. Truck driver positions approved through the program rose from 1,584 in 2018 to 8,101 in 2024 before dropping in 2025, per a national wire service review published Nov. 1, 2026.


What it means: those are approvals, not hires, but they show how heavily some fleets lean on this channel. Any rule change hits a lot of seats.


And the rules are changing. On Nov. 6, 2026, Employment and Social Development Canada said new low-wage stream LMIAs can run up to two years, up from one.


The bigger shift comes March 1, 2027, if provinces opt in. In larger and mid-size metro areas, low-wage access would be targeted to occupations identified through the federal occupational projection system, plus any a province adds. Rural communities keep full access.


Here's the trucking catch. The federal Canadian Occupational Projection System rates transport truck drivers as "balance" nationally for 2026-2035. Not shortage.


As we read the release, a low-wage LMIA for a big-city terminal could depend on your province adding truck drivers to its list. Confirm with immigration counsel. Higher-wage offers fall under a different stream.


What it means: the GTA terminal may lose a hiring channel. A rural yard may keep it. That's a location decision, not just an HR one.


## The retirement wave is already here


"Balanced" doesn't mean easy.


The same federal projection counts 330,600 transport truck drivers employed in 2025, with 43% aged 50 or older. It projects 133,800 job openings from 2026 to 2035, mostly from retirements, against about 111,400 new job seekers. New immigrants make up about 40.6% of those projected seekers.


What it means: replacement, not growth, drives demand. And in Ontario, newcomers face the longest path. Applicants from non-reciprocal jurisdictions must pass a G2 test and then a G test at least 12 months later, per the Sept. 21 release. Then comes the six-month Class A wait.


Meanwhile, capacity is shrinking. A November 2026 freight market update cited an equipment research estimate that Canada's tractor count was 2.9% below a year earlier. Load board data in the same update had Canada-to-U.S. loads up 31% year over year in October.


What it means: freight is coming back faster than seats. Fleets with qualified drivers in March will have pricing power. The rest will be turning down freight they just bid on.


## What you actually decide this week


Back to the whiteboard. Here's how your 14 candidates sort out.


-


**December road tests.** Book slots now for candidates who are ready and whose Class G is under six months old. Only the ready ones.


-


**Licence status by candidate.** Record full G date, Class A test date, province of licence, restrictions and months of Class 1 experience. That's what tells you when each seat is real.


-


**Quebec movers.** Plan the SAAQ practical exam into onboarding for anyone with under 24 months of Class 1 who's moving to Quebec. Staff a backup driver for the lane's first month.


-


**Alberta restrictions.** Flag provincially restricted Class 1 drivers. Block them from interprovincial dispatch until the restriction is gone.


-


**School evaluation.** Ask every new licensee for training hour records. Thin files get a longer finishing program.


-


**Location strategy.** Ask counsel what March 1 means for each terminal's metro area before you plan any LMIA hiring.


-


**Customer commitments.** Match truck counts to seats you can prove, by month.


Final count: five drivers solid for March, three by May, one by summer. You call sales and push part of the Quebec start to April. It's an awkward call. It beats promising trucks you don't have.


## Make your system match your drivers


No two fleets qualify drivers the same way.


One runs Alberta-only work on restricted licences. Another runs Toronto to Montreal dedicated. A third hires newcomers whose overseas experience Ontario no longer fully credits.


The fleets that get through 2027 won't be the ones with the biggest recruiting budget. They'll be the ones whose systems know who can legally drive what, and where.


Driver records that carry licence class, restrictions, province and experience dates. Statuses that separate "licensed" from "dispatchable." Dispatch rules that stop a restricted driver from getting an interprovincial load. Permissions that keep a planner from overriding them. Capacity views that tie customer commitments to seats you can prove.


That setup work is unglamorous. It's also what keeps a new lane from opening with an empty seat.


## FAQ


### When does Ontario's six-month Class A waiting period start?


Ontario's six-month waiting period applies to Class A road tests taken on or after Jan. 1, 2027. Applicants need six months of full Class G (or a higher class that permits Class G vehicles) before they can take the test, though they can complete training, medicals and knowledge tests during the wait.


### Do Ontario truck drivers moving to Quebec have to retest?


Ontario Class 1 holders with under 24 months of Class 1 experience must pass Quebec's practical exams to exchange their licence for a Quebec one, under measures in place since July 2026. Quebec describes the rule as temporary.


### Can a new Alberta Class 1 driver haul freight outside Alberta?


Not right away. Drivers licensed under Alberta's Class 1 Learning Pathway get a licence restricted to Alberta until they complete a Competence Building Program of 10 to 18 hours of one-on-one training.


### What would Alberta's Bill 43 change for carriers?


Bill 43 would raise maximum fines for major commercial vehicle incidents from $10,000 to $50,000, allow commercial licence downgrades and let the province publicly name non-compliant carriers, drivers and schools. It was introduced Nov. 19, 2026, and isn't law yet.


### How do the 2026 Temporary Foreign Worker changes affect trucking?


Low-wage LMIAs can now run up to two years, and from March 1, 2027, low-wage access in larger metro areas may be limited to targeted occupations if provinces opt in. Truck drivers are rated "balanced," not shortage, in the federal projection, so check your terminal's location with immigration counsel.
